blocks.text: At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs at the horse and its rider] The sense is that God so deprived this bird of wisdom that he nevertheless provided for its safety and preservation, since it is not easy for a man, even a horseman, to overtake it. At the time when: כעת, or κατὰ καιρὸν [kata kairon], when the time has come; so the Greeks, Jerome, Pagninus, the Genevans, etc., which is how it seems to be taken in Num. XXIII, 23. Otherwise כעת is more often joined with what follows, as כעת מחר, at the time of tomorrow, 1 Sam. IX, 16, and passim; כעת מנחת ערב, at the time of the evening offering, Dan. IX, 21; כעת הראשון יקל, At the time when the first was light, Esa. VIII, 23. So here I prefer, with the Chaldee, to take it as At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs, etc., because the two hemistichs cohere better this way. It lifts itself on high] In Hebrew במרום תמריא. Because the word תמריא occurs only here, the ancient interpreters explain it variously. [II, 868] The Syriac has ܬܬܬܪܝܡ ܐܝܟ ܕܩܠܐ, and the Arabic likewise ترتفع مثل النخلة [tartafiʿ mithl al-nakhla], It is raised up like a palm, as if תמריא thamri alluded to תמר thamar, that is, to the palm. This is absurd, since in תמריא the Thau is servile. The Chaldee, however, has טיסא, it flies. And the old Scholiast on this passage: Ἐν τῇ πτήσει τὸ θαῤῥεῖν ἔχουσα ἵπταται [En tē ptēsei to tharrhein echousa hiptatai], Trusting in its flight it flies. Jerome better: it raises its wings. The Seventy best of all: ὑψώσει [hypsōsei], it will be lifted up. For the ostrich does not fly, since it is incapable of flight; rather it raises its wings on high, or rather it is itself lifted on high. That is, when hunters approach the nest, it rises from its resting place and towers up beyond belief through the tallness of its stature and the stretching out of its neck, which is aptly signified by the word תמריא. For it is the future of Hiphil, and the Kal is מרא mara; which, with the letters transposed, seems to have been formed from ראם raam, that is, to be high. For we have proved elsewhere ^{e)} that רום rum and ראם raam mean the same ^{(5)}. So by these words, it is raised on high, the tallness of the ostrich's stature is commended, about which writers say much. Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, at the end of the fourth book: Τὸ μέγεθος οὐκ ὄρνιθος ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τετράποδος [To megethos ouk ornithos echei, alla tetrapodos]· It has the size not of a bird but of a quadruped. Diodorus, book 2: Τὸ μέγεθος ἔχουσι νεογονεῖ καμήλῳ παραπλήσιον [To megethos echousi neogonei kamēlō paraplēsion]· It has nearly the size of a newborn camel. Oppian, in the third book of the Cynegetica:
Τῆς ἤτοι μέγεθος μὲν ὑπέρβιον, ὅσσον ὕπερθεν Νώτοις εὐρυτάτοισι φέρειν νεοθήλεα κοῦρον· [Tēs ētoi megethos men hyperbion, hosson hyperthen / Nōtois eurytatoisi pherein neothēlea kouron·]
